subject: Computer Networking
title: Networking in Space
description: A quick, practical guide to Networking in Space.

hook.text: Mars is 20 light-minutes away. TCP can't work — a 40-minute wait per acknowledgment is unworkable.

buildup.text: DTN stores data at each hop until the next node is reachable. Built for intermittent, lossy links.

discovery.text: NASA tested DTN on the ISS. It handles disconnections gracefully, unlike TCP.

twist.text: Interplanetary links face huge signal loss. A Mars signal is billions of times weaker than cellular.

climax.text: As we reach the Moon and Mars, we need an interplanetary internet. Design is underway now.

punchline.text: Space networking rewrites every rule. New protocols for a new frontier.

quiz.question: Why can't TCP work well for Mars-to-Earth communication?
options: The 40-minute round trip for acknowledgments makes TCP impractical
Mars doesn't have enough bandwidth for TCP packets

details.summary: Space networking connects satellites, ground stations, and deep space probes using protocols adapted for extreme distances and delays. Delay-tolerant networking handles latencies of minutes to hours for interplanetary communication.
details.whyItMatters: Space networking enables humanity's expanding presence beyond Earth. The protocols and techniques developed for space networking also advance terrestrial networks dealing with disruption and delay.
takeaways: Delay-tolerant networking handles minutes to hours of latency
Laser inter-satellite links create space backbone networks
TCP fails in space because it assumes short round-trip times

faq.question: Why doesn't TCP work in space?
faq.answer: TCP assumes round-trip times of milliseconds and interprets long delays as congestion, drastically reducing throughput. A Mars round trip takes 4 to 24 minutes.

faq.question: How do satellites communicate with each other?
faq.answer: Traditionally through radio links to ground stations. Modern constellations like Starlink use laser inter-satellite links that beam data between satellites in orbit at the speed of light through vacuum, which is actually faster than fiber optic. This creates a space-based backbone network.
